content: The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group (PCG) contributed to the development of the guideline by defining the scope of priority questions and overseeing the updating of relevant systematic reviews. These updates adhered to the standard processes established by the Cochrane Collaboration. Methodologists from the Centre for Research Excellence in Pregnancy (CREP) evaluated the evidence from these systematic reviews using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. In cases where no suitable systematic reviews existed, either Cochrane or non-Cochrane, new systematic reviews were commissioned to address the priority questions and considerations relevant to the guideline. This document represents the World Health Organization’s (WHO) commitment to supporting evidence-informed policies and practices globally. It was developed following the standard operating procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process included identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing the evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updating of the guideline. The WHO Steering Group, composed of staff from the Department of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), supervised the guideline development process. This group drafted the initial scope of the guideline, identified priority questions and outcomes, prepared the guideline planning proposal, and selected systematic review teams, guideline methodologists, and members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). They also oversaw evidence retrieval, assessment, and synthesis, organized GDG meetings, prepared draft recommendations for review, finalized the guideline document, and managed its publication and dissemination. The GDG was formed by 18 external experts and stakeholders from six WHO regions, representing diverse expertise in research, clinical practice, policy, and program implementation related to intrapartum care. This group also included two patient/consumer representatives. A short biography of GDG members was made publicly available for review and comment before the first GDG meeting. Selected members participated in a scoping meeting in April 2016 to provide input on the guideline’s framework. The GRADE evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks were developed in collaboration with experts from CREP, Argentina, the University of Central Lancashire, and King’s College London, alongside the WHO Steering Group. These frameworks were informed by new systematic reviews of quantitative and qualitative studies. Representatives from external organizations, such as FIGO, ICM, RCOG, UNFPA, and USAID, were invited to the final GDG meeting in September 2017 as observers, given their potential role in implementing the guideline. The WHO Steering Group conducted a rigorous scoping exercise to identify and map clinical practices, interventions, and health outcomes related to intrapartum care. This process began with a scoping literature review to define the population of interest and explore the concept of “normal” labor and childbirth across various settings. A preliminary literature search of existing clinical guidelines and key systematic reviews was also performed, utilizing sources such as the Cochrane Database, PubMed, and professional society web pages. This exercise identified approximately 140 potential interventions applicable during the intrapartum period, from labor admission to the immediate postpartum period. To prioritize outcomes, 44 international experts and stakeholders in maternal and child health were invited to rank the importance of identified outcomes using an electronic survey. The median scores were calculated to classify outcomes as “critical” (median scores ≥7) or “important but not critical” (median scores 4–6). These prioritized outcomes informed the development of the guideline framework, which was discussed at a scoping meeting in Geneva in April 2016. The meeting aimed to prioritize guideline questions and define the scope in terms of focus, population, interventions, and outcomes. The guideline’s scope was limited to essential interventions applicable in low-, middle-, and high-income settings and relevant to all pregnant women, regardless of their risk status at the onset of labor. Highly specialized interventions for managing complications, such as labor dystocia or fetal distress, were excluded. The focus was on essential intrapartum care practices that all pregnant women and adolescent girls should receive to ensure a positive childbirth experience. Evidence to support the guideline was derived primarily from Cochrane systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The WHO Steering Group collaborated with the Cochrane PCG and CREP methodologists to identify relevant Cochrane reviews addressing the prioritized questions. Outdated reviews were updated in accordance with Cochrane PCG standards. In cases where no systematic review existed, new reviews were commissioned from external experts, who were required to prepare a standard protocol before initiating the review. The integration of recommendations from existing WHO guidelines was also a key component of this process. Recommendations published since 2012 and approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) were included. These recommendations covered critical aspects of intrapartum care, such as the third stage of labor, immediate newborn care, and postpartum care for women. They were integrated without modification, as they were considered current and relevant. The guideline emphasizes evidence-based practices for routine care and the management of complications, actionable information systems, functional referral systems, effective communication, respect for dignity, emotional support, competent human resources, and the availability of essential physical resources. It aims to achieve a positive childbirth experience, defined as one that meets or exceeds women’s personal and sociocultural expectations, ensures the birth of a healthy baby in a safe environment, and provides continuity of practical and emotional support from skilled and compassionate clinical staff.
